It also has the oddity `.ends(['published'], () => 'published')` in the doc flow.

B's chains are less consistent. Some builders take arrays (`.lanes([...])`, `.recalls([...])`) and others take varargs, and adapters take positional `(kind, dir, map)` arguments. A is uniform: varargs and option objects throughout. A also has fewer concepts to learn for this scenario (no access, reaction, playbook.recall policy or schedule `c.order`).

Surface: A measures 200 and B 250, and both cover 10/10. B adds entities A does without: `H.access`, `H.decision`, `H.resource`, `H.metric`, `H.threshold`, `H.retry.*`, `H.time.*`, a mailbox with four event states, `Lane.unit`/`Lane.event` makers and `console()`. A covers the same battery with `H.halt`, `H.on.metric` bounds and one `H.policy.retry`.

Durable framing: A gets restart, preemption and failure from fewer mechanisms. It has one `.recovery` on commands, `Driver.recover` for agents, `startState` on preemption, and one `Lane.retry` policy with held units. B needs `restart` per step, the `escalate`/`ask`/`probe` variants, `retry(policy, { exhausted })` and `failsTo`, plus a four-case mailbox consumption rule. B's own design notes admit it 'has four cases where the parent had two'.

Scenario 4 needs fewer pieces in A. Slack is an observer, and placement plus preflight live on the command (`.on(hosts, pick).preflight(diskSpace)`). B needs an extra trigger, `incidentTransitions` with `.invokes(incidentNotice)`, and `.preflight` on the lane, which duplicates it across `backups` and `renewals`.

B's `epicFlow` calls `.spawn('decompose', features, ...)`, so the flow names another lane and that lane's kind. This breaks principle 13 ('Flows stay blind to other kinds') and introduces the hidden coupling principle 10 warns against. A's flow exposes only a typed `outlet: 'feature'`, and the lane's `spawns:` config maps it to `features.unit(...)`, which keeps the relationship on the pivot.

A puts the failure move on the kind (`.failsTo(Abandoned)`) and the retry bound on the lane, and documents the default (no `failsTo` means unbounded backoff at pending). This reads principle 12's failure default literally. B adds a second failure destination, `.retry({ exhausted: GaveUp })`, beside `onAttemptFailed`. That forces an extra `GaveUp` state into the Bug and Feature lifecycles and makes a lane without a failure destination a startup error, which leans away from 'by default a failed attempt leaves the unit at pending'.

On durability, A ties capacity strictly to position. Halt and spawn keys must map to `Waiting<St>`, and kernel blocks go to a declared `blocked:` state. Each startup check is enumerated. B's 'a blocked attempt holds no capacity, whatever its unit's position' lets the attempt status contradict the unit's position on the board, which principle 12 defines on positions.

B's 06 memory scope uses raw strings in place of entity references: `when: { kinds: ['Draft'], roles: ['critic'], resources: [`section:${draft.section}`] }`. A connects the same memory through the entities themselves with `when: { kinds: [Draft], tags: [section.is(...)] }`, so the `section` tag is one dimension used for both metrics and recall scope, not two words for one thing.

B keeps a per-call `RunOptions.scope` (`ctx.run(reviewerA, input, { scope })`) beside tags. It also has untyped `ctx.children(): UnitView<unknown, string>[]` and a fallback string `a.model ?? 'unknown'`. A derives recall scope from attempt tags, types `ctx.children(features)` per lane, and makes `AgentResult.model` required, which removes the hidden coupling.

A anchors shared quota on the account instance through `QuotaPartition` (`cc.subscription(name, { token, quota })`). B uses a `sharedQuota` string option on `sqlite.ledger`, which ties account state to the ledger backend by path, a weaker pivot under principles 8 and 15.

In scenario 9 one `H.on.metric(read, { trip, reset, minSamples })` source per trigger expresses the hysteresis that A spreads across metric, threshold, `crossed` and `recovered`.

In scenario 9, B's `approval-audit` trigger handles both the trip and the reset in one closure (`event.state === 'reset' ? act.move(audits, key, 'audit-withdrawn') : ...`). A needs four triggers (`opensAudit`, `withdrawsAudit`, `pausesConversations`, `resumesConversations`), an `events({ recovered })` declaration on Audit and a reaction to express the same thing.

B's design notes cut methods that no scenario uses (`Lane.retry`, `H.policy.recall`, unused view fields). A adds `trippedAt` plumbing and `console()` on top of a larger builder vocabulary (`mark`, `exit`, `ends`, `opens`, `sets`, `skips`), so a newcomer has fewer names to learn in B.

Surface is 200 against 250 with the same 10/10 coverage. B's FlowContext (`run`, `halt`, `wait`, `spawn`) replaces A's `step`/`batch`/`halt`/`spawn`/`loop`/`sets`/`exit`/`ends` chain, and B needs none of A's mailbox apparatus (pending/postponed/applied/consumed, `Repeated`, `progress`, `opens`, `halts`, `skips` maps) to express the same durable re-entry.

In scenario 04, B's Slack alert is an observer (`slack.notify({ message })`) and its incident halts reuse active phases. A needs an extra trigger (`incidentTransitions` with `.invokes(incidentNotice)`), separate waiting states `AwaitingAcknowledgement`/`AwaitingResolution` mapped through `halts:`, and an `opens:` entry per lane.

A's design admits the merge raised the consumption rule from two cases to four ("What the merge costs in honesty"). B's durability story is replay plus per-command `.recovery` and `Driver.recover`, with fewer named mechanisms: kernel halts `H.halts.definitionChanged` and `costCeiling` stand in for A's six block reasons and its `manageAttempts`/`skips` machinery.

A makes every connection a named pivot. `H.agent('release-reviewer').role(reviewer).model(...).pool(H.pool('release-subscription')...)` states which pool serves which agent. B registers `.pools(pool)` on the harness and leaves the kernel to work out which pool serves `reviewer` versus `summarizer`, a hidden coupling a newcomer cannot see.

In B's scenario 10, the Release flow reads another kind's states as raw strings: `children.every((child) => child.state === 'passed')`. That is the flow secretly knowing the Smoke kind. A's spawn returns `ChildResult.verdict`, and the lane maps the result through `exits: { released: Released, smokeFailed: SmokeFailed }`, so neither flow knows the other's states.

A declares restart behaviour on each step, next to the effect it guards: `afterCrash: 'rerun' | 'park' | 'askDriver'`, `alreadyDone: announcementPosted`. Recovery from a changed definition is a granted `H.ops.attemptsRecover`. B splits the same vocabulary across `Command.recovers`, `Executable.recovery` and `Model.recover`. Its definition-changed restart is reachable only through the generic `resolveHalts` operation.

A's builder chains read uniformly as `H.kind(...).attributes().states().key().initial()` and `H.lane(...).supply().store().handler(flow, { exits, during, params })`. B mixes a flow phase string ('backingUp'), a kind state string ('backup-failed' in `failsTo` and `H.on.enters`) and a state descriptor (`backingUp`) for one concept, so a reader must hold three namings at once.

In 04-ops, A states each rule by its name: `.admit(backups, ctx => ctx.active(incidents) === 0)` and `ssh.host(...).slots(1).preflight(diskSpace)`. B hand-writes a scheduler that sorts, filters and preempts inside `incidentsFirst`, and its Slack observer needs an imperative `entry.entry === 'transition' && entry.kind === Incident.name` string check.

B's positional `H.trigger(name, source, (event, act) => ...)` and `H.clock(name, Kind, spec, produce)` with manual dedupe keys (`${service}@${now.toISOString()}`) need more explanation than A's chained `.on(H.when.pattern(...)).create(lane, ...)` and `H.clock(...).every({ minutes: 5 })`.

Ergonomics under the durable framing is about whether a reader can predict how execution behaves from the scenario lines. In A's scenario 6, `editor: WithEditor` maps the halt to a waiting state, so the capacity effect can be read straight off the lane config. In B, `WithEditor = H.state('WithEditor', 'active')` is paired with an attempt that is 'blocked holding nothing'. A reader must learn that position and attempt status diverge before they can predict what the board and the WIP count will show.

A names the A/B swap through owner-defined metrics on the decision entity: `H.metric('acted-on-first').of(editorCall).hit(...)`, read with `c.metrics.read(ownMetric, { agent: own, ... })`. That line reads as what it does. B's `critiqueActedOn` hand-builds a `Sample[]` keyed on `event.models.critiqueFirst` model-name strings, then adds a `weakerIncumbent` helper that compares `firstIncumbent.name` strings. That is more machinery to explain and more raw strings standing in for entities.

B's chains are smoother in places: variadic `.states(...)`, `H.when.step(..., { if })`, and the scheduler builder `.priority().wip().boost()`. But B's scenario 6 needs a four-key `during` map that repeats `InReview`, plus a separate `.metrics(critiqueActedOn)` registration. A's `states: { factCheck: Reviewing, editor: WithEditor, ... }`, together with `records(tasteJournal, ...)` on a typed `e.outputs.editor?.notes`, needs fewer things explained.
